History:
• Presenting complaint: New onset wheeze and shortness of breath for 2–3 days.  
• Course: Day-time breathlessness on walking; sometimes unable to finish sentences. No breathlessness at rest; can climb stairs.  
• Associated symptoms: Dry cough, subjective “fever” (home temperature 37 °C), no sputum, no hemoptysis, no chest pain, not woken at night.  
• Past similar episodes: Childhood and adult asthma; last significant use of medication reportedly 3–4 yrs ago, though patient also states using salbutamol “every few weeks” (conflict noted).  
• Triggers: Possible pollen exposure; no recent infection confirmed.  
• Social/functional impact: Unable to walk to work; working from home or on sick leave.

Past Medical History:
• Asthma – childhood onset; required inhalers; occasional hospital visits (no ICU).  
• Hay fever; eczema.  
• Allergies: No known drug allergies.  
• Medications: Salbutamol inhaler – dose/route/frequency not documented (reported “every few weeks” and for exercise). No other regular medicines.  
• Surgical history, family history, immunizations: not discussed.

Physical Examination: (video/telephone)
• General: Alert, conversant, no distress while seated.  
• Respiratory: Reports wheeze on exertion; none at rest during call.  
• Vitals: Temperature 37 °C (home reading). No other vitals provided.  
• No chest pain; able to speak in full sentences during consultation; occasional difficulty previously reported.

Impression:
Likely acute asthma exacerbation, possibly pollen-related or viral-triggered.

Management Plan:
• Increase salbutamol to 2–4 puffs every 4 hours as needed.  
• Prescribe spacer device for improved inhaler delivery; pharmacist to demonstrate use.  
• Prescribe/issue peak-flow meter; patient to record readings morning and evening for 1 week.  
• OTC regular antihistamine recommended for allergic component (pharmacist to advise).  
• Safety-netting: If temperature rises, wheeze worsens, or breathlessness increases, contact service immediately.  
• Follow-up: Telephone or face-to-face asthma review in 1 week with peak-flow diary; earlier if deterioration.

Patient Summary:
A 33-year-old engineer with childhood asthma now presents with a 2-3-day flare of wheezy breathlessness affecting exertion. No red-flag features at rest. Managed as an acute asthma exacerbation with stepped-up reliever use, spacer, peak-flow monitoring, antihistamine, and scheduled review.

Key Takeaways:
• Use salbutamol 2–4 puffs via spacer every 4 h while symptomatic.  
• Start daily antihistamine from pharmacy to limit allergic triggers.  
• Record peak-flow readings twice daily and return for review in 1 week—or seek help sooner if symptoms worsen or fever develops.

Next Steps:
• Collect spacer and peak-flow meter from pharmacy; obtain demonstration.  
• Maintain peak-flow diary.  
• Arrange asthma follow-up appointment in 1 week with results.  
• Consider stepping up to maintenance inhaler after review pending peak-flow data.

Quality checks (document_quality):
• Missing expected elements: objective vitals (HR, RR, SpO₂), full medication list reconciliation, family history, surgical history.  
• Internal conflicts: Patient states asthma meds stopped 3–4 yrs ago vs current salbutamol use every few weeks.  
• Transcript quality: Clear; minor repetition and incomplete addresses; no impact on clinical data capture.
